newsitem.title: USA: Black legislators want U.S. Army investigated.
newsitem.headline: Black legislators want U.S. Army investigated.

text.p: Black legislators called on Wednesday for Congress to investigate allegations by five white Army women that they were forced by military investigators into accusing black instructors of rape.

"We certainly want to make sure that any instances of sexual harassment or rape ... are rooted out and stamped out of our military," Representative Harold Ford, a Tennessee Democrat, said at a news conference. "But at the same time we want to make sure that race and racism are rooted out as well."

The 39 members of the Congressional Black Caucus asked military committees in both the Senate and the House of Representatives to conduct independent investigations of the allegations made on Tuesday by five women Army recruits at Aberdeen Proving Ground in nearby Maryland.

The five women soldiers told a news conference on Tuesday that Army investigators tried to bully them into accusing superiors of rape. Four said they refused. One said she accused a sergeant of sexual misconduct but recanted.

The Army has charged three instructors and a captain at Aberdeen with rape and four instructors with sexual harassment on the basis of allegations by nearly 50 women in the Army, including 27 who charged they were raped.

The eighth soldier was charged earlier on Wednesday. Staff Sgt. Herman Gunter, 30, was charged with two instances of rape as well as sexual harassment, assault, adultery and obstruction of justice in cases involving three trainees.
The news conference by the five women soldiers was sponsored by the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People and several NAACP officials called for an independent investigation.

Army Secretary Togo West said at a House hearing on Wednesday he would consider it but was concerned that an independent investigation might interfere with court-martial proceedings at Aberdeen in the Army sex scandal.

"We don't want to have another situation in which our prosecutions get thrown out unless they are for good reason," West said. "If it turns out there was abuse then of course it should not go forward. But we want to make sure that we don't disrupt the ongoing proceedings."

Representative Maxine Waters, chairwoman of the black caucus and a California Democrat, said the congressional investigations should not interfere with the court-martial proceedings, unless Congress decided they were so badly contaminated that it must take action to stop them.
Nearly 50 Army drill sergeants and other leaders are under investigation for sexual harassment or rape of trainees at Aberdeen and Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri.

Army officials have also said more than 7,000 calls were made to a special sexual harassment telephone hotline set up after the first Aberdeen charges were filed. They said about 1,025 of the hotline allegations were being investigated.
